entries.title: Germany news: Calls intensify to ban Meta Glasses
entries.summary: Both rights groups and regulators say the new AI tech is dangerous to consumers. At the same time, debate is heating up over pension reforms. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Calls intensify to ban Meta Glasses

August 3, 2026

Both rights groups and regulators say the new AI tech is dangerous to consumers. At the same time, debate is heating up over pension reforms. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • So-called "smart glasses" have ignited fierce controversy in privacy-conscious Germany
  • The Bundestag may reopen negotiations on pension reforms after criticism from some conservative leaders

Here are the latest headlines, reports and analyses from across Germany on Monday, August 3: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

Skip next section Privacy advocates and regulators alike call for Meta Glasses ban

Privacy advocates and regulators alike call for Meta Glasses ban

According to German digital rights NGO HateAid, police in the city of Potsdam have already received complaints from young women who say they were filmed by male strangers at a public swimming pool using Meta Glasses.

Germany is known for being a highly privacy-conscious country, and photographing and filming strangers without their consent is against the law. However, as HateAid points out, the burden of proof often rests on the victim. Moreover, with Meta Glasses, it is much less obvious when one is being recorded than with a smartphone.

"This technology is fueling digital violence, as perpetrators now need virtually no technical know-how," HateAid said.

Thomas Fuchs, a privacy and digital regulation official for the city of Hamburg  , told broadcaster ARD that he thinks an outright ban on smart glasses is possible.

Meta's main German corporate offices are located in the northern city-state.

His office tested the glasses, he said, and found that the LED light that is supposed to alert passersby that a user in filming is far too faint to be see in normal daylight.

He told ARD that he is speaking with colleagues in Ireland, where Meta has their European headquarters, on crafting policy at the EU-level.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from a sweltering, sunny Bonn.

Today we will be looking at the protracted debate over when Germans will be allowed to retire, as well as concerns over new tech critics say breach fundamental rights.

Stay with us for coverage of all the headlines in Germany today.

entries.title: Myanmar: Aung San Suu Kyi meets Red Cross official, junta says
entries.summary: Myanmar’s military-led government released images from the 81-year-old Nobel laureate’s meeting with ICRC’s resident representative for Myanmar, Arnaud de Baecque.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

Myanmar’s military-led government released images from the 81-year-old Nobel laureate’s meeting with ICRC’s resident representative for Myanmar, Arnaud de Baecque.

Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday, marking one of the only publicly confirmed contacts between the 81-year-old Nobel laureate and an outside party since the military ousted her government in February 2021.

The meeting, held in the capital Naypyitaw with ICRC resident representative Arnaud de Baecque, was announced by Myanmar'smilitary-backed government, which released four photographs of the encounter.

What do we know about the meeting?

Two images show Suu Kyi shaking hands with and meeting de Baecque in a sparsely furnished room. The government did not disclose further details of what was discussed.

Two other photos offer a rare glimpse into her circumstances: Suu Kyi is shown cutting a pink birthday cake in what appears to be her residence, with a clothes rack and storage boxes visible in the background. The cake's inscription — "Happy Birthday Aunty Suu" — suggests the images may have been taken around her 81st birthday in June.

While it could not be independently verified when or where the photos were taken, AFP said AI analysis found no signs the images were fabricated.

When was Aung San Suu Kyi last seen in public?

Suu Kyi has had no confirmed public sightings since her 2021 detention, and her exact whereabouts and details about her health have been difficult to determine. She is serving a 27-year sentence on charges her allies say were politically motivated.

In late April, following elections that installed former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing as president, authorities said her sentence had been commuted by one-sixth as part of a broader prisoner amnesty and that she had been moved from prison to house arrest.

Despite that shift, the new administration has largely resisted outside access to her. A May request from the Philippines, on behalf of the regional Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) bloc, to allow a special envoy to visit Suu Kyi was turned down.

Pressure for access has been building from other ASEAN members as part of broader efforts to resolve Myanmar's political crisis, now compounded by a civil war that followed the coup.

Suu Kyi's younger son, Kim Aris, who lives in London, has led an online campaign with Myanmar democracy activists demanding proof that his mother is alive and in good health, saying he has gone years without hearing from her.

Myanmar's junta said in December that she was "in good health."

The ICRC did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the meeting, according to Reuters.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections
entries.summary: Ahead of four elections in Germany this fall, dozens of fake posts are circulating online aimed at discrediting candidates and portraying Germany as divided. Analysts warn that Russia is now targeting local candidates.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections

August 3, 2026

Ahead of four elections in Germany this fall, dozens of fake posts are circulating online aimed at discrediting candidates and portraying Germany as divided. Analysts warn that Russia is now targeting local candidates.

Eric Stehr was unsure what to think when he first saw fake videos about himself.

He describes his reaction as "mixed feelings," somewhere between amusement and concern, laughter, and helplessness. "I don't want something like that online," he told DW. "But at the same time, I know there's nothing I can do about it."

A German student, Stehr is running for the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt as a candidate for the socialist Left party. Being second on the party list, he has a good chance of winning a seat in the election on September 6.

But social media posts about him have falsely claimed that:

The false reports have been cleverly designed so that they appear to come from major German media outlets, including the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Stern TV, ARD and Spiegel TV. But the videos are as false as the allegations they make.

A spokesperson for the police confirmed to DW that Stehr is not under investigation and has not been suspected of murder. Meanwhile, a Bauhaus University Weimar spokesperson confirmed to DW that there are no reports of alleged university sex parties or an alleged grading scandal.

More than 180 fake posts ahead of elections

According to DW Fact Check findings, the videos are part of the Russian influence operation known as Matryoshka, also referred to as Operation Overload. DW Fact Check has identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok ahead of the upcoming elections.

The data comes from a detailed archive maintained by the anonymous investigative collective Antibot4Navalny, which was originally founded to expose disinformation targeting late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny and now tracks Russian influence operations online.

DW reviewed several fake posts published since June 24. Notably, the campaign operates only on weekdays, with disinformation activity dropping off on weekends.

Many of the posts target candidates running in the upcoming German elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Lower Saxony and Berlin, all scheduled for September. The votes are seen as an indicator of Germany's political mood and a test for the country's recently reshuffled federal government.

Operation Matryoshka reaches new level

Observers were not surprised to see Germany become a target of the campaign, but the scale of the operation has raised concerns.

"This influence campaign has been active across multiple platforms since September 2023," said Julia Smirnova, researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS). "Its targets have included Germany's federal election, elections in Moldova and Armenia, and the Olympic Games in France."

What is new, Smirnova said, is the focus on relatively obscure individual candidates in local elections. "It is unusual for Russian influence campaigns to target specific candidates in regional elections." According to her observations, candidates from all parties have been targeted, except for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

"What we're seeing now ahead of the state elections is a continuation of Russia's long-term strategy: Supporting parties perceived as more Russia-friendly while discrediting other parties and candidates," said Smirnova.

Pablo Maristany de las Casas, a specialist in foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns at the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), sees similar patterns. Like Smirnova, he says the narratives mirror earlier Russian influence operations. The messages, he argues, are once again "pro-Russian, anti-German and anti-EU."

Who is behind Operation Matryoshka?

While no definitive link to the Russian state has yet been established, there is evidence that Russian-speakers are behind some of the posts, according to Maristany de las Casas. For example, a Spanish-language post on X was found to contain a revealing clue: The post, which targeted candidates Lydia Hüskens and Andreas Silbersack of the Free Democratic Party (FDP), abbreviated their party's name as "SvDP," which would the Russian version: Svobodnaya Demokraticheskaya Partiya.

The OSINT research group Gnida Project, which investigates Russian disinformation campaigns, has previously linked Matryoshka to Russian actors. According to its findings, the operation is technically and operationally connected to Storm-1516, a well-known unit reportedly controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, and which was also active in the lead-up to Germany's federal election in 2025.

For Smirnova, the evidence points strongly in one direction. "With a very high degree of probability, this is a Russian campaign carried out on behalf of the presidential administration," she said, before adding that such operations are often executed by private companies specializing in digital marketing and political influence campaigns.

How can Matryoshka fakes be distinguished from real media reports?

The fake videos are professionally produced, but small inconsistencies often reveal that they are imitating established media brands.

Key questions can help identify manipulated content:

  • Is the video published on an official account belonging to the media outlet?
  • Do the design and typography match the outlet's actual branding?
  • Where does the footage come from, and does it support the story being told?
  • Does the video present any verifiable evidence for its claims?

In the current wave of fakes, these questions quickly expose a familiar pattern: Fabricated stories, stolen footage, cloned logos, and imperfect copies of genuine video formats. Many of the discrepancies become apparent only upon closer inspection.

What narratives are being spread ahead of the elections?

The campaign's messaging broadly falls into two categories.

Discrediting candidates: In one case DW spotted a video about Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner (archived video on archive.org) of the Christian Democrats (CDU), in which he is falsely accused of murdering a professional tennis player. The voice of the video is AI-generated and no evidence is provided. Berlin police confirmed to DW that no professional tennis player had recently been killed in the city and that there are no investigations involving Wegner.

Candidates from the CDU, the Social Democrats (SPD), Greens, the Left Party, and the FDP have also been targeted with false allegations of corruption, drug use, and, in dozens of cases, fabricated sex scandals.

Deepening divisions between eastern and western Germans: One fake video masquerading as a Eurostat report (archived video on archive.org) claims that a large majority of western Germans consider reunification a "historic mistake." The supposed survey is not described in any detail, and no evidence of its existence can be found.

In a statement to DW, Eurostat said: "This is a fake video. Eurostat did not produce it. Eurostat did not conduct the "survey" mentioned in the video." In fact, genuine polling paints a different picture of western Germans sentiments: According to an ARD DeutschlandTrend survey from October 2025, 64% of respondents in western Germany said they were satisfied with the state of German reunification.

Numerous other posts claim that eastern Germans face systematic discrimination, that eastern Germany receives less investment in security and infrastructure, or even that experts predict a new division of Germany by 2030. One video goes so far as to claim there are plans to build a new Berlin Wall. None of these claims are true. Some posts even use the hashtag #TimeToDivideGermany.

"The goal is to pit eastern and western Germans against one another, or to suggest that people in eastern Germany are despised, hated, or discriminated against by western Germans," Smirnova said. "It is also about harming specific politicians through false accusations."

How effective is the disinformation campaign?

The operation remains active, with new fake content appearing regularly, but experts interviewed by DW say the campaign's impact appears limited so far. "The impact is really not that significant, as we can see from this artificial amplification of content," Maristany de las Casas said.

Many posts receive tens of thousands of views, sometimes more than 100,000, yet generate little genuine engagement. Comments, shares, and other interactions remain relatively low, and previous research suggests that disinformation campaigns such as Matryoshka/Overload have achieved only modest influence.

Another reason may be platform moderation. Unlike X, platforms such as Bluesky and TikTok often remove the content relatively quickly.

Eric Stehr, however, does not want to rely on that. He plans to file a criminal complaint over the fake videos. His attempt to have one of the videos removed from X was unsuccessful, he said, because the platform said it "saw no reason to take it down," and for now, the disinformation campaign targeting German politicians continues.

Additional reporting by Asya Lokina, Aldo Sanchez Vera and Anwar Ashraf.

Edited by Ben Knight

entries.title: Iran denies talks with US underway after Trump comments
entries.summary: US President Doanld Trump president said a fresh round of talks to end to the war would begin on Monday. Iranian authorities later dismissed the statement, saying they are only in talks with Oman. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran denies talks with US underway after Trump comments

Published August 3, 2026last updated August 3, 2026

US President Doanld Trump president said a fresh round of talks to end to the war would begin on Monday. Iranian authorities later dismissed the statement, saying they are only in talks with Oman. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • US President Donald Trump said new round of Iran talks set for Monday

  • He made the statement after calling of attacks on Iran

  • Iran says there are no talks underway with Washington

  • Two tankers with Saudi oil exit Red Sea

This blog covers the latest developments in the US-Israel war with Iran and the wider fallout across the Middle East on Monday, August 3.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Iran hangs two convicted of espionage

Iran hangs two convicted of espionage

Iran says it executed two men on Monday after they were convicted of spying for Israel.

It is the latest in a series of hangings on espionage allegations carried out by Tehran since the start of the war with Israel and the US in late February.

"Omid Behzad and Pouria Safvat were hanged this morning for transmitting the coordinates of sensitive military and security sites to Mossad agents," said Mizan, the media outlet for Iran's judiciary.

Mossad is Israel's foreign intelligence service.

"They helped the intelligence services achieve their objectives by providing them with information on military and security centres during the war," Mizan added.

Executions in Iran as a whole have risen since the war broke out.

According to Amnesty International and several other rights groups, the country carries out the second-highest number of executions in the world, after China.

At least 1,639 people were executed in Iran last year, a record high since 1989, according to the Norway-based NGO Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty (ECPM), which has its headquarters in Paris.

Skip next section Oil slumps on hopes of Iran deal

Oil slumps on hopes of Iran deal

Oil prices fell sharply in early Asian trading after US President Donald Trump announced new talks with Iran aimed at ending the Middle East conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude for September delivery dropped more than 6% to $82.41 a barrel in early trade.

The conflict has disrupted energy markets and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and gas shipment

Skip next section No current talks with US — Iranian Foreign Ministry

No current talks with US — Iranian Foreign Ministry

Iran is not currently conducting talks with the ‌US, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said on Monday, adding that it is, however, in discussions with Oman about a temporary safe route through the Strait of Hormuz.

The remarks by ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei came after US President Donald Trump said new talks with Iran on a peace deal were set to begin on Monday.

"We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," Baghaei said during a weekly press briefing.

He added that a deal with Oman would not be enough to reopen the strait for commercial shipping, as the situation would stay unchanged if the US continued with its "aggression."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

We are continuing our coverage on the US war with Iran and broader developments in the Middle East after US President Donald Trump said he had called off strikes on the West Asian country.

He later told reporters that Washington and Tehran were to carry out new talks on Monday. There was no immediate response from Iran.

Meanwhile, some Saudi oil ships passed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait despite a stated embargo by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia.

Stay with us for all this and more.

Skip next section Some Saudi oil shipments get through Bab el-Mandeb

Some Saudi oil shipments get through Bab el-Mandeb

Two tankers carrying Saudi crude successfully crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait over the weekend, despite security concerns and a Houthi-declared maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia.

Shipping data showed traffic through the waterway fell sharply amid the heightened security risks, with just 18 commodity vessels passing on Sunday, down from 28 on Friday.

The tankers, Lesvos and Desh Vaibhav, transited with their Automatic Identification System (AIS) tracking systems switched off, the Kpler data showed. Together, they were carrying about three million barrels of Saudi oil.

Desh Vaibhav is heading to India's Sikka port, while Lesvos' destination remains unclear.

Meanwhile, vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz also slowed, with commodity crossings dropping after reports of multiple tanker attacks.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency says three more attacks have been reported since Saturday, raising fresh concerns over the security of key global energy shipping routes.

What is the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis?

The Houthis are an Iran-backed militant group that has controlled most of Yemen's more populous areas — including the capital, Sanaa — for a little over a decade.

A coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the country's internationally recognized government, which is de facto based in the southern city of Aden.

While the Saudi-backed government agreed to a truce with the Houthis in 2022, this year tensions have risen again amid the US war with Iran.

Skip next section Trump says Iran talks to resume amid push to reopen Strait of Hormuz

Trump says Iran talks to resume amid push to reopen Strait of Hormuz

US President Donald Trump said new talks with Iran are set to begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the Islamic republic to pursue a deal to end the war.

"They said we would much prefer a deal as opposed to an attack, because you don't know where these attacks lead," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One late on Sunday.

He was looking for a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and address concerns over Tehran's nuclear program.

He gave no details on the venue, participants, or any deadline for an agreement.

The comments followed a social media post in which Trump said Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had requested more time to complete a deal.

Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike.

Iran and the United States agreed in mid-June on a framework deal to end the war, with details to be finalized during a 60-day transition period, but both sides have since carried out major attacks.

entries.title: Cuba suffers yet another nationwide blackout
entries.summary: Cuba's electricity grid has collapsed again after three nationwide blackouts in July. The power failure comes amid a US-imposed oil blockade on the communist island.
entries.content:
Cuba

Cuba suffers yet another nationwide blackout

August 3, 2026

Cuba's electricity grid has collapsed again after three nationwide blackouts in July. The power failure comes amid a US-imposed oil blockade on the communist island.

 Cuba's state-owned grid operator said the island's power system collapsed late on Sunday, the latest in a series of rolling power cuts caused by aging infrastructure and a US energy embargo.

The outage comes on the heels of three nationwide power outages last month.

What do we know about Cuba's latest blackout?

The state-run utility UNE said there was a "total disconnection" of the national electricity system, which means the entire country of 10 million people, including the capital, Havana, has been plunged into darkness.

The Ministry of Energy said that protocols to reactivate the grid were underway.

The series of outages afflicting the island in recent times have also affected water supplies and cooling systems, making normal life extremely difficult.

Cuba, which relies largely on aging oil-fired power plants, lost access to fuel from its previous primary supplier, Venezuela, after US President Donald Trump imposed an oil blockade following Washington's ouster and capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on January 3.  

Imports from Mexico, which subsequently became Cuba's key supplier of oil, have also ceased under US pressure.

Supplies brought by a single Russian tanker in March with Washington's authorization have been exhausted.

Cuba has also been under a broader US embargo for decades.

Stepped-up US campaign against Cuba

Cuba is also facing other pressure from the US, including ramped-up sanctions against Cuban state-owned businesses imposed by the Trump administration.

These have led to a number of foreign companies suspending their operations in the island.

Washington has also indicted former President Raul Castro over the downing of two civilian planes 30 years ago, in which three US citizens and a US resident died. 

The US redesignated the communist island as a "state sponsor of terrorism" for a third time in 2025, shortly after former President Joe Biden moved to have it deleted from the list.

Trump has even made scarcely veiled threats to take over the island.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Spain's wildfires: Counting the economic cost
entries.summary: Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent the flames?
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent the flames?

Charred tree stumps, melted asphalt, burned-out cars and destroyed buildings: The wildfires in southern Europe are leaving a trail of devastation and causing billions of euros in damage.

Spain's economy in particular is at risk of being choked by clouds of ash. According to the EU's Copernicus Earth observation system, around 206,000 hectares of forest in Spain have already gone up in flames this year.

"According to the European Commission, the economic impact of wildfires in Spain in 2022 amounted to approximately €7.1 billion ($8.1 billion), representing around 4.5% of the country's GDP. This figure reflects not only the direct costs of firefighting but also the long-term economic consequences of recovering the affected areas," Emilio Vizuete Luciano, an economist at the University of Barcelona, told DW.

The fires often devastate the local economy and disrupt trade in the affected regions, Luciano says. "Tourism is also severely affected. Given Spain's strong dependence on tourism, the disappearance of this activity in fire-affected regions has particularly significant economic repercussions."

Wildfires slow economic growth

Climate economist Sarah Meier of Swiss public research university ETH Zurich has taken a closer look at the economic losses caused by wildfires in southern Europe. Her findings show that in regions affected by at least one wildfire, the growth rate fell by between 0.11% and 0.18%.

According to a 2023 study she co-authored, the decline in growth was even greater when several wildfires occurred simultaneously, rising to as much as 4.5% depending on the extent of the fires. "Our calculations are an average for the period from 2011 to 2018," she explains.

And she issues a stark warning: "The costs become particularly high when wildfires reach larger cities, something that has so far been very rare in southern Europe."

The European Environment Agency (EEA) has also calculated the economic losses caused by wildfires in previous years. In 2017, when nearly 990,000 hectares burned across southern Europe, the losses amounted to almost €10 billion. 

Europe is burning

According to the European Commission, the EU loses around 500,000 hectares of land to wildfires every year. Spain, Greece and France are among the countries where wildfires are most widespread.

The economic damage goes far beyond losses to tourism. It also includes the loss of biodiversity, declining forestry revenues, soil erosion, destroyed infrastructure and property, as well as the costs of fighting the fires.

A heated debate has erupted in Spain over the cost of fighting wildfires. Since 2009, investment in prevention has actually been declining — even though the number and scale of wildfires have reached alarming levels over the past decade.

According to official figures, spending on wildfire prevention in Spain fell from €364 million in 2009 to €144 million in 2024. Over the same period, annual spending on actually fighting and extinguishing fires remained stable at around €417 million.

For economist Luciano, there is "a certain irony" to this because prevention has been proven to be the best long-term investment. "It is far cheaper than fighting wildfires once they have already broken out."

Spain's high cost of firefighting

The Spanish forestry services company Forescat has estimated that fighting and extinguishing wildfires costs around €19,000 per hectare. Nearly 400,000 hectares of forest went up in flames in Spain in 2025, amounting to costs of around €7.6 billion.

It's still too early to say how much fighting this year's fires will cost Spain; however, Maria Inmaculada Marmol Tardaguila of MATS, a social organization representing public-sector healthcare workers, says things cannot continue this way.

"Continuing to rely on the heroic efforts of firefighting crews to keep our forests safe is both ecological recklessness and fiscal irresponsibility," she notes on the organization's platform, which has also warned of an increase in respiratory illnesses caused by wildfire smoke.

"The solution is not to keep buying more and more firefighting aircraft, but, for example, to remove combustible material such as deadwood from forests before the first spark catches," she points out.

Unless public officials understand this, she warns, Spain will continue to "burn through its budget at the same rate as its forests burn."

This piece was originally published in German.

entries.title: 5.0 magnitude earthquake strikes Egypt
entries.summary: The quake occurred at 3 a.m. local time about 22 miles north ⁠of the Egyptian city of Suez, the US Geological Survey said.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

The quake occurred at 3 a.m. local time about 22 miles north ⁠of the Egyptian city of Suez, the US Geological Survey said.

A magnitude 5.0 earthquake struck off Egypt early on Monday, according to the United States Geological Survey.

The quake happened at 3 a.m. local time (0000 ​GMT) and hit an area about 22 miles (36 kilometers) northeast of the seaport city of Suez. 

The ​German Research Centre ‌for Geosciences (GFZ) measured the earthquake at magnitude 5.4 and ​recorded the depth of the quake at 6 miles (10 kilometers).

The Egyptian Red Crescent said it had activated ‌its emergency response plan in ‌the governorates where the earthquake was felt.

No immediate reports of damage or injuries

There were no immediate reports of casualties or property damage.

Humanitarian organizations urged residents to avoid buildings showing signs of structural damage.

Damaging earthquakes are uncommon in the northeast African country. The country's deadliest earthquake in modern history struck in October 1992, when a 5.8-magnitude quake shook the capital, Cairo, killing more than 500 people and displacing thousands.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Man arrested over death of British woman found in suitcase in Athens
entries.summary: The body of Scottish national Elisabeth-Jane Ross was discovered last month in a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

The body of Scottish national Elisabeth-Jane Ross was discovered last month in a suitcase in a derelict building in Athens.

A 26-year-old man has been arrested by Greek police in connection with the death of a British woman whose body was found in a suitcase in Athens last month.

"Officers of the Directorate for Combating Organized Crime have solved the homicide of a 38-year-old UK national, whose body was found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in the Kypseli area on July 18," the Hellenic Police said on Sunday.

Police say suspect confessed

The victim, identified in British and Greek media reports as 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane Ross from Scotland, arrived in Greece in late June and was last known to be in the Athens area on July 10. She was later reported missing.

Police said the suspect, a foreign national, confessed on Thursday and now faces charges including intentional homicide, robbery and firearms-related offenses.

"It emerged that the [suspect] placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned premises. Furthermore, in the days that followed, the 26-year-old used the victim's bank cards to withdraw sums of money," police said.

According to reports, the suspect said the victim was already dead when he found her, although police made no mention of this in their statement.

A replica pistol and a knife were recovered from the suspect's home.

Greek police said international cooperation, including support from Interpol authorities in the US and UK law enforcement agencies, helped identify the victim despite advanced decomposition.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Pakistan: Suicide bomber kills 14 at anti-militancy protest
entries.summary: A suicide bomber has killed over a dozen people including police in an attack during a demonstration of citizens against militancy. More than 18 people were injured in the attack.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Suicide bomber kills 14 at anti-militancy protest

August 2, 2026

A suicide bomber has killed over a dozen people including police in an attack during a demonstration of citizens against militancy. More than 18 people were injured in the attack.

A suicide bomber killed 14 people and injured dozens more in an attack targeting anti-militancy demonstrators in the city of Kabal in Pakistan's northwestern Swat Valley.

Five police officers were among those killed at the event, which was staged outside a local police station to protest growing militant violence in the region and the state's inability to protect citizens.

Those gathered accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants, saying residents want to live without fear after years of devastating violence.

The area was the home of Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai, who was shot there by a Taliban gunman in 2012.

Hundreds of people were at the rally and social media video footage showed a speaker mid-sentence when an explosion rocked the area and sparked panic among demonstrators.

"The suicide bomber blew himself up when asked for a search in front of the police station," a local police official said.

No group has claimed responsibility for the crime.

A former Taliban stronghold

President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif both condemned the attack.

"Terrorists," said Zardari, "will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity and the writ of the state."

Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks of late, with many targeting police and security forces.

The Swat Valley was a Taliban stronghold between 2007 and 2009, when Pakistan's military drove the Islamists out and re-established government control over the area.

The religious militants have recently resurfaced, however, with the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, being particularly active.

The TTP is separate from, but allied with, Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has been a source of tension between the neighboring countries.

Pakistan says the TTP and other militant groups are carrying out attacks in the country with the support of Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has promised to continue targeting the TTP and its support network.

Europe

Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia, killing eight

August 2, 2026

Ukrainian drone strikes inside Russia killed eight people overnight in attacks that targeted military and civilian infrastructure. Russia said Moscow's forces downed 635 drones in the assault.

Ukrainian drones rained down on numerous military, energy and civilian infrastructure sites deep inside Russia on Sunday, killing at least eight people overnight.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 635 drones over the course of the attacks.

Two people were killed in the city of Engels on the Volga River when drones hit residential buildings. Another apartment complex in nearby Saratov City was also damaged.

Three people were reported killed and two injured in the Udmurtia region (1,300 kilometers from Ukraine), and another three killed and five injured in Belgorod according to local officials.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said Kyiv had targeted an oil refinery in Saratov and a military base that is home to Russian long-range bombers in Engels.

Zelenskyy said the attacks were his country's answer to Russian aggression and thanked Ukrainian forces for taking the war "back to where it came from."

Kyiv said fires had damaged both sites and that its forces had also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region.

Unverified video uploaded to social media sites purported to show fires burning at the Saratov oil facility.

Why is Ukraine targeting Wildberries warehouses?

Ukraine again targeted the online retailer Wildberries in its attacks, striking a logistics warehouse in Samara — more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) from Ukraine's front-line positions.

Sunday's attacks on Wildberries were just the latest onslaught on the retail giant, which Kyiv says aids Russia's military.

Kyiv has attacked nearly a dozen Wildberries warehouses since July 18.

No casualties were reported at the facility and local management said that a fire at the site had been brought under control.

Although the number of drones that Russia claims to have downed cannot be confirmed, the figure is indicative of the scale of Kyiv's effort to strike Russia deep inside its own territory as it defends itself against an army that launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

The Wildberries attacks are seen as an attempt to bring President Vladimir Putin's war home to Russia's citizens, applying pressure to the country's already anaemic economy in hopes of finally ending Moscow's ongoing invasion.
